types.name: Asset
types.doc:
Base class for all assets in the Asset Pipeline.
Inherits RefCounted for automatic lifetime management via Ref<T>.
Two-phase loading: Load() for CPU data (any thread), CreateGPU() for GPU resources (main thread).

members.name: CreateGPUBudgeted
members.signature: virtual bool CreateGPUBudgeted(const GPUContext& ctx, int budget)
members.doc:
Time-sliced GPU creation for the async-import drain. MAIN THREAD
ONLY. Does up to `budget` GPU work units (<= 0 = unbounded / one-shot).
Returns true once the asset reached a TERMINAL state — GPUReady on
success or Invalid on failure — and false while more budgeted work
remains for a following frame. The default is one-shot (a single
CreateGPU); large assets (meshes) override it to yield across frames.

members.name: EstimatedUploadBytes
members.doc:

footprint estimate, which a texture knows from its CPU data alone; a
type whose estimate needs its GPU objects (a mesh) overrides it.

members.doc: Destroy GPU resources. Must be called on main thread.

members.name: DestroyGPUIsFrameSafe
members.doc:
True when DestroyGPU only drops RHI objects whose backends already hold
their release until the frames in flight have retired (images do, on
every backend). A reimport of such an asset needs the render thread
fenced, not the whole device drained — the drain was a multi-second
freeze in a Debug editor each time an artist saved a texture.

members.name: CanAdoptLoadedState
members.doc:

so the loader cannot simply hand back a new one: it parses into a fresh
object of the same type and the main thread moves that CPU state into
the live one, after Unload and before CreateGPU. A type that cannot say
which of its members Load fills keeps the synchronous reimport.

types.name: AssetHandle
types.doc:
AssetHandle<T> — wrapper around Ref<T> that supports pending UUID resolution.
An asset handle can be in one of three states:
1. Empty — no UUID, no asset
2. Pending — has UUID, asset not yet loaded/resolved
3. Ready — has a valid Ref<T> to the loaded asset

Usage:
AssetHandle<TextureAsset> handle(someUUID);  // pending
handle.Resolve(assetManager);                 // try to resolve
if (handle.IsReady()) { handle->DoSomething(); }

The one load-by-path verb a caller below the editor/runtime split can
use: hands back the asset only when it is fully resident, otherwise
starts (or continues) loading it off the calling thread and returns
null. Poll it — the frame it returns non-null is the frame to use the
asset. Repeat calls for one path coalesce into one load. The base
only probes the cache, which is what a bare manager in a test wants.

applying its authored slot materials does it on the main thread, inside
the GPU drain. The base resolves them now, which is what a packaged
game with cooked textures wants; the editor imports what is missing in
the background and binds each slot as its texture lands, instead of
decoding every slot of every material in the one frame a model finishes.

types.name: MatNodeType
types.doc:
Node-based material authoring. A MaterialGraph is a set of expression
nodes feeding a single Material Output node whose input slots map to the
fixed PBR channels the renderer already consumes (base color, metallic,
roughness, normal, emissive, AO, opacity + the extended flags). The graph is
stored inside the .mdfmat next to the flat PBR fields. There are two compile
products: EmitCompiledShader emits a real per-material HLSL evaluator the
cook compiles into per-graph blobs, and Compile() folds the same graph down
to the flat fields, which stay the fallback whenever a blob is missing.
Texture-sample nodes assign a texture slot; constant/param/math nodes
constant-fold into scalar/vector channel values.

members.name: VertexColor

too, so a graph that only multiplies by it is identity by default.

members.name: MakeMaterialAttributes
members.doc:
Layered materials (UE's material layers). These two node kinds carry a
whole surface along the wire instead of a float4 — a "layer bus". A
MakeMaterialAttributes packs the seven PBR channels into one; a
LayerBlend crossfades two of them under a mask, and chaining blends
stacks arbitrarily many layers. Every layer compiles into the SAME
per-material shader (one draw, one pipeline, no extra push bytes and no
descriptor churn) — the whole point of the feature is that N layers
cost one pass, not N.

The two buses are NOT interchangeable: a float4 wired into a layer pin,
or a layer wired into a float4 pin, is refused at compile time rather
than silently coerced. Coercion would produce a material that renders
plausibly and wrongly, which is the failure this rejection exists to
prevent.

Fields reused so serialization stays untouched: MakeMaterialAttributes
takes its unconnected-pin fallbacks from the same out*/color fields the
Output node uses; LayerBlend's `scalar` is the height-blend transition
width in height units (only read when the Height pin is connected).

members.name: MaterialFunctionCall
members.doc:
Material functions (UE's MaterialFunction). A call node names a
`.mmatfunc` asset by path (functionPath) and exposes one input pin per
Function Input node the function declares, in that function's node
order; its single output is the function's Function Output. The call is
INLINED at compile time — MaterialGraph::Resolve splices the function's
nodes into the caller with fresh ids and rewires the pins — so the
emitter, the fold and the WPO bound walk never see a call at all and a
function costs exactly what its body costs. Recursion (a function that
reaches itself through any chain of calls) is refused with an error
that names the cycle; without that check the resolver would expand
forever.

Inside a function: FunctionInput carries the pin name in paramName, its
unconnected-caller default in `color` (a scalar input reads .x) and its
type in scalarPin; FunctionOutput takes the result on slot 0 and names
it in paramName. Reached outside a function (the function editor's own
compile) an input reads its default and an output passes through.

members.name: StaticSwitch
members.doc:
Static switches (UE's StaticSwitchParameter). A StaticSwitch picks
True (slot 0) or False (slot 1) at COMPILE time from the StaticBool
wired into its Value pin (slot 2), or from its own boolValue when the
pin is unwired. The unselected branch is never visited: it emits no
code, takes no texture slot and no parameter lane. Every NAMED
StaticBool is one permutation axis — 2^N shader permutations, each
its own source and hash, bounded by r.Material.MaxStaticPermutations.
A material instance overrides the bool by name and thereby selects
its permutation. An unnamed StaticBool is a constant, not an axis.

members.name: SubstrateSlab
members.doc:
Substrate: a second BSDF slab layered over the material's own surface.
A slab is albedo / F0 / roughness / normal / coverage, and layering one
over another is what the fixed shading models cannot express — each of
them spends the single custom G-Buffer scalar on a different thing, so
clear-coat-over-cloth has nowhere to live.

Slice 1 encodes exactly two slabs and the bottom one IS the ordinary
surface (RT0/RT1), so this node authors the TOP slab. There is still no
VERTICAL stacking node: with two encodable slabs and the bottom one taken,
stacking two authored slabs needs three and every use would be a compile
error. That waits on the payload target —
Documentation/ROADMAP.md §12.4.

Coverage/Roughness/F0 are pins; the albedo is a two-bit codebook on the
node (maskChannel) because sixteen bits cannot hold an independent RGB.
The slab shares the base slab's normal for the same reason.

members.name: SubstrateBlend
members.doc:
Two slab definitions crossfaded under a mask, resolving to ONE slab
before the encode. This is the side-by-side case, not the vertical one:
its output is a single slab by construction, so it cannot produce a stack
that does not fit and needs no extra G-Buffer bits. What it buys is a coat
whose CHARACTER varies across the surface and not only its thickness — ice
on the ledges and powder in the crevices of one rock, wax on a jacket's
shoulders and bare fuzz elsewhere — which today needs two materials and a
mesh split.

The albedo codebook entry is the one thing it cannot blend: the mode is
two bits baked into the shader as a define, so the emitter refuses a blend
whose two slabs disagree about it rather than silently keeping one.

members.name: SceneDepth
members.doc:
Scene inputs (UE's SceneDepth / CustomDepth / CustomStencil): the scene's
device depth, the custom depth pass's depth and its stencil value at the
evaluated pixel. Pin 0 is an optional screen UV (defaults to the
pixel's own). Live in the post-process domain, where the pass binds the
three targets; the surface domains carry no frame block for them and
read zero. Fold to zero — a screen-space value has no constant.

types.name: FSubstrateCodec
types.doc:
The two-slab G-Buffer codec, mirrored from Engine/Shaders/Private/Lighting/
Substrate.hlsli. Slab 0 is the ordinary G-Buffer; this describes slab 1,
which rides the sixteen bits the tier-7 escape frees from clear-coat duty.
The shader and this struct are pinned against each other by the
substrate-codec-test row — a bit layout with two writers and no test is how
the anisotropy nibble drifted before it was centralised.

members.name: ExtendedSlot
members.doc:
Tier 7's low five bits name an extended slot; slot 1 is Eye, so
Substrate takes slot 2 and shading-model id 9. Renderer/Material.h has
no EShadingModel entry for it yet (that header is outside the material
path), so this is where the reservation lives.

not describe the same eye.

compiling the defaults over them unconditionally would straighten a
hand-authored stare on the next unrelated graph edit; while this is
false the compiler leaves the material's own values alone.

members.doc:

pass (GBuffer, shadow, velocity, forward, meshlet) evaluates the same
clamped offset, so tightening the derived cull bound to min(derived,
maxWpo) can never cull geometry the shader still displaces. The one
way to re-arm the geometric kills on a graph whose derived bound is
the unbounded sentinel. Participates in the shader hash (it changes
the emitted code), like every other Output-node constant.

members.doc:
Whether a node kind carries a layer bus (FMaterialAttributes) rather
than a float4. Mixing the two is a compile error, not a coercion.

members.name: IsSubstrateNode
members.doc:
Whether a node kind carries a Substrate slab. A third bus, kept apart
from the layer bus for the reason the two exist separately at all: a
horizontal layer blend crossfades seven PBR channels, a slab blend
crossfades three slab fields, and a wire that could be either would
compile and render plausibly and wrongly.

members.name: SubstrateAlbedoMode
members.signature: uint32_t SubstrateAlbedoMode(uint64_t nodeId, uint64_t& mismatchNode) const
members.doc:
The albedo codebook entry a slab subtree resolves to, following blends
down to their inputs. mismatchNode receives the id of the first blend
whose two sides disagree (kNoErrorNode when they all agree) — the mode is
two bits baked into the shader as a define, so a disagreement is a hard
limit and not something to average. Shared with the editor so the
diagnostic and the compile error can never drift apart.

members.name: FoldSubstrateTop
members.signature: uint32_t FoldSubstrateTop(uint64_t nodeId, bool& outVaries) const
members.doc:
The authored slab reduced to ONE packed G-Buffer word, or 0 when it does
not reduce (outVaries set). Two consumers cache a single answer per
surface rather than shading per pixel — the GI surface cache stores one
colour per card texel, and the ray-traced hit shading blends against that
cache — so both need a slab that is constant over the material. A graph
whose coverage rides a texture has no such word, and answering 0 there
leaves those two paths shading the base surface exactly as they did
before Substrate existed. That is a visible gap, not a silent one: the
material editor says so on the node, because an average coat invented
here would make a snow line bounce snow-coloured light into the crevices
it does not reach.

types.name: MaterialGraph::ShaderStats
types.doc:
Offline HLSL codegen. EmitHLSL walks the output node's connected inputs
and emits a self-contained material function
(FMaterialOutputs EvaluateMaterial(FMaterialInputs)) into the same
template the GBuffer material path would #include. Real per-graph shader
variant compilation through DXC is not wired at runtime — this is the
authored artifact the cook would compile. EstimateStats returns the
instruction/sampler counts the editor shows.

types.name: MaterialGraph::FGraphParam
types.doc:
Compiled-material emission (the path `mbt` actually compiles, unlike
the free-standing EmitHLSL preview): texture nodes are assigned the
GBuffer material descriptor slots 0..7 in first-use order (deduped by
texture UUID), and the emitted code samples the MatGraphTexN/
MatGraphSampN aliases GBufferFill.hlsl defines under MATERIAL_GRAPH —
so the per-material shader keeps the exact pipeline layout of the
uber-shader and only the evaluation differs. Textures carries the
UUID for each used slot, in slot order; the renderer binds them into
the material descriptor set in the same order. Hash is FNV-1a of the
emitted source — the shader's stable identity for the cook, the cache
and the runtime lookup ("Materials/<hash-hex>").
R4: a NAMED Scalar/Vector parameter no longer constant-folds into the
source — it compiles to a read of a parameter lane the renderer feeds
per draw, so changing the value never recompiles the shader. Unnamed
param nodes keep folding (they are constants with a param-shaped node).

Lane layout. A graph whose parameters fit the ORIGINAL four-lane block
keeps that block's exact packing — vectors take whole lanes from the
front, scalars pack four per lane from the BACK — and reads them as
In.Params[lane]; its emitted source is byte-identical to what it was
before the ceiling was lifted, so every cooked blob, committed sidecar
and shader hash stands. A graph that does not fit takes the WIDE
layout: vectors from the front, scalars four per lane immediately
after them, up to kGraphParamLanesMax lanes; lanes 4 and up read
MatGraphParamsExt[lane - 4], a static array the emitted source declares
(zero unless the pass template fills it), and the source announces its
width with `#define MATERIAL_GRAPH_PARAM_LANES <n>` so the templates
and the upload can size their copy by the graph instead of by four.
The instance override path addresses lanes by name -> (lane, comp)
through this table, never by position.

members.name: wpoBound
members.doc:
Conservative interval bound on |EvaluateWorldPositionOffset| in world
units, evaluated under the vertex-stage input contract (UV/normal/
view read zero, vertex color in [0,1], time unbounded but folded
through sin/saturate/noise). The meshlet task stage inflates its
cluster cull spheres by this so per-cluster frustum/Hi-Z kills stay
sound under displacement; kWpoBoundUnbounded means the subtree could
not be bounded (e.g. it scales with WorldPosition) and every
geometric kill must be skipped instead. 0 when the graph has no WPO.
An authored Output-node maxWpo (> 0) tightens this to min(derived,
maxWpo) — sound because the same value is baked into the evaluator
as a magnitude clamp, so no pass can displace past it.

both of them rendered before Substrate existed; substrateVaries says
whether that 0 means "none authored" or "authored, but it moves per

types.name: MediaSourceAsset
types.doc:
MediaSourceAsset (.mmedia) — a clip plus how it should play, the way UE's
MediaSource + MediaPlayer settings pair.

FMediaPlayer::Open already takes a path, so why an asset: a bare path is not
a reference. It cannot be renamed with a redirector, it does not appear in
the dependency graph, and the cook has no way to know a movie is used — so a
packaged build ships with the cutscene missing and nothing says so until a
player reaches it. Naming the clip through an asset puts it on the same
footing as a texture or a mesh.

The playback settings live here rather than at each call site because they
belong to the CLIP: a looping ambient screen and a one-shot cutscene want
different answers, and the answer should travel with the content instead of
being re-decided by whoever opens it.
